s0201.literal: When he first pacified Hou Jing, and when he established Shaotai, children, jade, and silks were all distributed to officers and soldiers.
s0201.idiomatic: After he first subdued Hou Jing and again when he set up the Shaotai regime, sons and daughters, jade, and silks were all shared out among his officers and soldiers.

s0202.literal: Those who filled the inner quarters wore no double brocade; ornaments had no gold or kingfisher; song-bells and female musicians were not arrayed before him.
s0202.idiomatic: Those in the inner quarters wore no doubled brocade; ornaments bore no gold or kingfisher feather; bells and female musicians were not set before him.

s0203.literal: When he ascended the throne, he was even stricter in respectful frugality.
s0203.idiomatic: Once he took the throne, he was stricter still in modest frugality.

s0204.literal: Therefore his lofty merit and abundant virtue shone over all under Heaven.
s0204.idiomatic: Thus his towering merit and rich virtue held sway over the realm.

s0205.literal: Yao Cha, Director of the Ministry of Personnel of Chen, said: The Founder's heroic strategy was broad and magnanimous; in meeting change he had no fixed method—he was next only to Han Gaozu and Wei Wu.
s0205.idiomatic: Yao Cha, Chen Director of the Ministry of Personnel, said: The Founder's genius was vast and his bearing magnanimous; he met every turn without a set plan—only Han Gaozu and Cao Cao could stand beside him.

s0206.literal: When the western capital was overthrown, his sincerity pierced Heaven and man.
s0206.idiomatic: When the western capital fell, his loyalty ran through Heaven and earth.

s0207.literal: Wang Sengbian lacked Yiyin's talent yet vainly nursed the grievance of the Tung Palace; Zhenyang borrowed the escort of Qin troops yet did not think of Mu Ying's weeping.
s0207.idiomatic: Wang Sengbian lacked the gift of an Yiyin yet brooded on the wrong of the Tung Palace; Zhenyang leaned on northern troops yet never remembered Mu Ying's tears.

s0208.literal: The Founder then trod the dark mystery to comfort the declining age, seized the gap in the tide to rescue the crosscurrent—the royal foundations began here; how could it be only the victory of defeating the Li people and ascending Yang?
s0208.idiomatic: The Founder then walked the hidden Way to steady a dying age, caught the breach in the flood to save the realm—the throne's roots began here; it was far more than the triumph at Li and the ascent of Mount Yang.

s0209.literal: Therefore in the age of careful compliance with the seasons and proper sequence, at the time of changing sounds and altering things, the myriad people returned in song; the blazing spirit departed as if a burden were lifted—compared with former ages, how beautiful!
s0209.idiomatic: In that age of careful ritual and renewed order, when music and customs were remade, the people sang him home and the old mandate slipped away like a load set down—set beside earlier dynasties, how fine a founding it was!

s0211.literal: The Emperor, your subject Baxian: the two characters "Baxian" originally read "taboo name"—this preserves Yao Cha's old text; as an official historian of Liang and Chen, he observed the Chen taboo.
s0211.idiomatic: On "your subject Baxian": the text originally read "taboo name," preserving Yao Cha's wording; as a Liang and Chen historian he avoided the imperial name.

s0212.literal: The Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions have all changed "taboo name" to "Baxian"; the present text follows them.
s0212.idiomatic: The Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions all read Baxian for taboo name; we follow them.

s0214.literal: And moreover matching songs of praise and litigation: "songs of praise and litigation"—the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions read "songs of praise."
s0214.idiomatic: On "matching songs of praise and litigation": the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions read "songs of praise."

s0217.literal: says: "Songs of praise and litigation carries the double sense of songs of praise and lawsuits at court; the character for litigation is not wrong."
s0217.idiomatic: writes: "Songs of praise and litigation combines popular acclaim with lawsuits at court; the word for litigation is correct."

s0218.literal: Since the age of misty chaos: "since"—the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions read "from the time of"; Yuan Gui 213 agrees.
s0218.idiomatic: On "since the age of misty chaos": the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions read "from the time of"; Yuan Gui 213 agrees.

s0221.literal: holds that reading "from the time of" is wrong.
s0221.idiomatic: argues that "from the time of" is mistaken.

s0224.literal: [Tong]—corrected according to all editions and Yuan Gui 213.
s0224.idiomatic: [Tong]—corrected per all editions and Yuan Gui 213.

s0225.literal: Comment: this alludes to Yiyin's placing Tai Jia at Tong; jiong and tong are graphically close and the former is a corruption.
s0225.idiomatic: Note: the passage uses Yiyin's exile of Tai Jia to Tong; jiong is a graphic slip for tong.

s0226.literal: Receiving the tally, famed defender: "defender"—all editions read "Yu"; Yuan Gui 213 reads "defender."
s0226.idiomatic: On "receiving the tally, famed defender": all editions read Yu; Yuan Gui 213 reads defender.

s0228.literal: Defender means commandery governor; "receiving the tally, famed defender" is the same as "receiving the tally, famed commandery."
s0228.idiomatic: Defender means commandery governor; the phrase means a governor enfeoffed by tally.

s0229.literal: If there are reed-marsh bandits: "reed" originally read "guan"; now corrected according to all editions; the same below.
s0229.idiomatic: On "reed-marsh bandits": the text originally read guan; corrected per all editions; likewise below.

s0230.literal: Comment: the reed of reed-marsh originally was written with the plant radical; the block was wrongly cut as guan.
s0230.idiomatic: Note: the reed character originally used the plant radical; the block misprinted it as guan.

s0231.literal: Governor of Yan Province: comment—in the previous juan Daotan was posthumously made Governor of South Yanzhou; here the character for South is missing.
s0231.idiomatic: On "Governor of Yan Province": the prior juan makes Daotan Governor of South Yanzhou; South has dropped out here.

s0232.literal: Marquis of Wukang county: comment—it should read "Duke of Wukang county"; see collation note 24 to the previous juan.
s0232.idiomatic: On "Marquis of Wukang county": it should be Duke of Wukang; see collation note 24 to juan 1.

s0233.literal: Opening those border passes: "open" was originally corrupted to "wall"; all editions are not corrupt; now corrected.
s0233.idiomatic: On "opening those border passes": the text originally read wall for open; other editions are correct; emended accordingly.

s0238.literal: was the first to hold this office: the character "Chang" is corrected according to the Northern Supervisory and Hall editions.
s0238.idiomatic: On "first to hold this office": Chang is restored per the Northern Supervisory and Hall editions.

s0239.literal: The character "chu" is deleted on Qian Daxin's argument.
s0239.idiomatic: The word chu is deleted following Qian Daxin.

s0240.literal: Comment—Qian Daxin's Examination of Discrepancies in the Twenty-Two Histories says: "Chang Yizhi in Liang times was North Xuzhou Inspector and once held the post of left and right valiant cavalry.
s0240.idiomatic: Qian Daxin's Examination of Discrepancies says: "Chang Yizhi served in Liang as North Xuzhou inspector and once held the left and right valiant cavalry post.

s0241.literal: The collator did not know that Chang Yizhi was a man's name, rashly added a mouth beside chang, and also inserted the character 'chu'—shallow and laughable."
s0241.idiomatic: The collator did not recognize Chang Yizhi as a personal name, added a mouth radical to chang, and inserted chu—a blunder worth laughing at."

s0242.literal: Liangzhou Inspector Zhang Li memorialized, saying, in the eighth month of the past yihai year: "past"—all editions read "said."
s0242.idiomatic: On "Liangzhou Inspector Zhang Li memorialized, in the past eighth month of yihai year": all editions read said for past.

s0245.literal: holds that reading "past" is correct; the yihai year was the first year of Shaotai of Emperor Jing of Liang—this refers to an earlier event, hence "past."
s0245.idiomatic: argues that past is correct: yihai was the first Shaotai year of Liang's Emperor Jing, an earlier date, hence past.

s0246.literal: South Yuzhou Inspector Shen Tai fled to Qi: "South Yuzhou"—the Basic Annals of Emperor Wenxuan in the Book of Northern Qi reads "Jiangzhou."
s0246.idiomatic: On "South Yuzhou Inspector Shen Tai fled to Qi": the Northern Qi Annals of Emperor Wenxuan read Jiangzhou.

s0247.literal: Comment—the Comprehensive Mirror follows the Book of Chen.
s0247.idiomatic: The Comprehensive Mirror follows the Book of Chen.

s0248.literal: Edict to Prince of Linchuan Qian for the western campaign: the character "Qian" originally read "taboo name"—so in Yao Cha's original text; now changed according to the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions.
s0248.idiomatic: On "Prince of Linchuan Qian, western campaign": the text originally read taboo name, as in Yao Cha; restored to Qian per the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions.

s0249.literal: Later cases of the same kind are not all given collation notes.
s0249.idiomatic: Similar cases below are not all annotated.

s0250.literal: Making Renwei General and Gaozhou Inspector Huang Fahe Grand Mentor with the Staff Equal to the Three Dukes—comment:
s0250.idiomatic: On "Renwei General, Gaozhou Inspector Huang Fahe made Grand Mentor with staff equal to the three dukes"—note:

s0252.idiomatic: reads General Who Proclaims Martial Valor.

s0253.literal: Advanced in title to General Who Pacifies the South—comment:
s0253.idiomatic: On "advanced to General Who Pacifies the South"—note:

s0255.literal: reads "General Who Pacifies the South"; the History of the Southern Dynasties here also reads "General Who Pacifies the South"—which is correct.
s0255.idiomatic: reads General Who Pacifies the South; the Southern Dynasties annals agree—correct.

s0256.literal: On jiawu day Guangzhou Inspector Ouyang Yi memorialized that a white dragon was seen on the south bank south of the province: "jiawu"—the Annals of Emperor Wu in the History of the Southern Dynasties reads "jiazi."
s0256.idiomatic: On "jiawu day, Guangzhou Inspector Ouyang Yi reported a white dragon on the south bank": the Southern Dynasties Annals of Emperor Wu read jiazi.

s0257.literal: The Hall edition's textual verification says: "According to the text above, on dingyou night there was great snow; then jiawu is two days earlier and should not be placed after.
s0257.idiomatic: The Hall edition notes: "The text above has heavy snow on dingyou night, so jiawu would be two days earlier and cannot come after.

s0258.literal: If the Southern Dynasties reads jiazi, checked against xinchou below, it again does not agree.
s0258.idiomatic: If the Southern Dynasties read jiazi, the xinchou that follows still will not align.

s0260.literal: Truly because the four acute ears did not reach: "reach" was originally corrupted to "far"; all editions are not corrupt; now corrected.
s0260.idiomatic: On "the four acute ears did not reach": the text originally read far for reach; other editions are correct; emended.

s0261.literal: A thousand li did not respond: "did not" was originally corrupted to "merit"; all editions are not corrupt; now corrected.
s0261.idiomatic: On "a thousand li did not respond": the text originally read merit for did not; other editions are correct; emended.

s0262.literal: Though the fields of Ying were prayed over: "prayed"—the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions read "thinned."
s0262.idiomatic: On "though the fields of Ying were prayed over": the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions read thinned.

s0263.idiomatic: Note: zhu here equals the word for prayer.

s0266.literal: holds that this uses the passage on praying for the millet fields in the Biography of Chunyu Kun in the Records of the Grand Historian, and it should read "prayed."
s0266.idiomatic: argues that the line echoes the millet-field prayer in the Biography of Chunyu Kun (Records of the Grand Historian) and should read prayed.

s0269.literal: lawsuits—deleted according to the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions and the Annals of Emperor Wu in the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0269.idiomatic: lawsuits—deleted per the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions and the Southern Dynasties Annals of Emperor Wu.

s0270.literal: The Founder's illness again grew severe—comment: the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions lack the character "again."
s0270.idiomatic: On "the Founder's illness again grew severe": the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions omit again.
